channel.title: Chrome Web Platform Ecosystem Updates
channel.description: Weekly web intelligence on ChromeStatus features, web standards, and developer community pulse

item.title: HTML-in-canvas — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
HTML-in-canvas (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

HTML-in-canvas enables customizing the rendering of html using canvas with new primitives to manage canvas layout, drawing capabilities, rendering events for DOM-to-canvas synchronization, and geometry update capabilities for canvas-to-DOM synchronization.

Ecosystem Analysis: The HTML-in-canvas specification addresses a long-standing web platform limitation by allowing live, interactive, and accessible DOM elements to be rendered directly into 2D, WebGL, and WebGPU contexts, officially shipping enabled by default in Chrome 157. It replaces fragile DOM-to-image workarounds like html2canvas, generating immense enthusiasm across the graphics and creative coding ecosystems. However, baseline interoperability remains limited because the specification is still undergoing incubation within the WICG and WHATWG review processes.

item.title: CSS text-decoration-inset — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS text-decoration-inset (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

CSS text-decoration-inset controls how far underlines, overlines, and line-through decorations are inset from or extended beyond text run edges. It supports auto, length, and percentage values, including one-value and two-value syntax for setting the start and end offsets. This lets developers adjust decoration spacing and create reveal effects with native text decorations instead of background gradients or additional elements. sampler: https://static.januschka.com/i-468928416/?asddsaasd MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/text-decoration-inset CL: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7748204

Ecosystem Analysis: CSS text-decoration-inset (part of CSS Text Decoration Module Level 4) provides native inline control to shorten, extend, or shift text decorations such as underlines and strike-throughs using lengths and percentages. The feature resolves a long-standing web typography pain point, replacing legacy workarounds like gradient backgrounds or pseudo-elements. With active implementation across Blink, Gecko, and WebKit, the property enjoys high cross-engine momentum and widespread standard alignment.

item.title: CSS flow-start and flow-end alignment keywords — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS flow-start and flow-end alignment keywords (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

Introduce the flow-start/end keywords as value aliases for the existing flex-start/end keywords as resolved in the CSSWG. These are needed for alignment in the case of placement reversals. flow-start in CSS Grid-Lanes would indicate the starting edge of the container at which placement begins, which is useful in the case where placement is reversed (`fill-reverse`, `track-reverse`, discussed in this CSSWG issue: [css-grid-3][masonry] item-flow row vs. column in masonry layouts · Issue #12803 · w3c/csswg-drafts). Because these are acting as value aliases, we expect flex-start/end to follow the logical directions in Grid Lanes, as well, which will expand the definition of these keywords from only applying special behavior in flexbox to applying to any layout mode whose logical start/end is different from its physical start/end. For serialization, if either flex-start/end or flow-start/end is used, the returned serialized value should be flow-start/end.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS flow-start and flow-end keywords introduce generic, placement-aware alignment values into CSS Box Alignment Module Level 3, serving as canonical aliases for flex-start and flex-end. They solve long-standing semantic friction and layout reversal challenges in modern specifications like CSS Grid Lanes (masonry), where item placement directions can invert relative to container logical edges. With Chrome shipping default support and Mozilla officially backing the design, engine alignment is rapidly solidifying around the CSS Working Group resolution.

item.title: Add javascriptURLs option to SanitizerConfig and Sanitizer — Chrome 159 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Add javascriptURLs option to SanitizerConfig and Sanitizer (Chrome 159, Enabled by default)

https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12898 Sanitizer API also sanitizes javascript:-URLs, when they are used for navigation. This was originally done as a side effect of any "safe" method that uses Sanitizer, and omittted for any "unsafe" method. The HTML standard recently regularized this and made this a developer-selectable option, instead of a side-effect of a particular method. Behaviour when the option is not used remains the same.

Ecosystem Analysis: The addition of the `javascriptURLs` option to `SanitizerConfig` and the `Sanitizer` interface regularizes the handling of navigation-related `javascript:` URLs, transforming what was previously an implicit side effect of 'safe' insertion methods into an explicit, configurable setting that defaults to disallowing them. The update reached swift tri-engine consensus in the WHATWG HTML repository to remove the awkward behavioral divergence between safe and unsafe HTML methods. With implementations rolling out across modern Chromium and Firefox releases and WebKit treating it as a natural extension of the broader Sanitizer API, the feature firmly solidifies native DOM sanitization semantics.

item.title: Support for WebHID — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Support for WebHID (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

The [WebHID API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/how-to/web-platform/webhid) enables web applications to interact with Human Interface Devices (HIDs) over USB and Bluetooth beyond standard system input mappings (such as mice, keyboards, touchscreens, and standard gamepads). Web applications can request user permission to connect to HID devices, send and receive input, output, and feature reports, and inspect report descriptors. WebHID shipped on [desktop platforms](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/capabilities/web-apis/hid-examples) (Windows, macOS, Linux, and ChromeOS) in Chrome 89. Chrome 158 brings the existing WebHID API to Chrome on Android (relying on new OS support in Android 17 / API level 37 and later) with no changes to the web-exposed API surface. Popular uses today include customizing mechanical keyboards, keypads, and gaming mice, calibrating gamepads, and integrating hardware headset call controls in call centers. WebView is not supported, as it does not have a device chooser UI or permissions UX controls. This feature can be controlled using the following enterprise policies: * [DefaultWebHidGuardSetting](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultWebHidGuardSetting) * [WebHidAllowAllDevicesForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAllowAllDevicesForUrls) * [WebHidAllowDevicesForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAllowDevicesForUrls) * [WebHidAllowDevicesWithHidUsagesForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAllowDevicesWithHidUsagesForUrls) * [WebHidAskForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAskForUrls) * [WebHidBlockedForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidBlockedForUrls) For more details, see [Set ChromeOS devices policies](https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/1375678) in the Chrome Enterprise and Education Help Center.

Ecosystem Analysis: WebHID enables direct web communication with human interface devices such as mechanical keyboards, specialized game controllers, and telephony headsets, originally shipping on desktop in Chrome 89 and expanding to Android 17 in Chrome 158. While Chromium continues broadening low-level peripheral access across platforms, the API remains classified as Limited Availability on Baseline. Cross-engine adoption is nonexistent due to fundamental architectural and security disagreements regarding raw hardware access on the open web.

item.title: Language Detector API on Android — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Language Detector API on Android (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Exposes the LanguageDetector JavaScript Web API on Chrome for Android (Clank). This allows web applications to detect text languages locally on mobile devices using fast, privacy-preserving, and offline-capable on-device machine learning models and not rely on cloud endpoints.

Ecosystem Analysis: Chrome for Android is shipping the Language Detector API enabled by default in Chrome 157, bringing mobile devices to parity with desktop by running compact on-device models for offline, low-latency language identification without cloud fees or heavy client bundles. However, the broader Web Translation and Language Detector specifications remain incubated in the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group without multi-engine consensus. While Chromium and Edge support the group's interfaces, Mozilla has registered an official negative position and Safari/WebKit has withheld formal endorsement, keeping baseline cross-browser interoperability strictly limited.

item.title: CSS4 text-decoration-skip-spaces — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS4 text-decoration-skip-spaces (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

The text-decoration-skip-spaces CSS property controls whether text decoration lines (underlines, overlines, line-throughs, etc.) skip over whitespace characters. This allows authors to prevent decorations from being drawn under spaces, which is often more visually appealing.

Ecosystem Analysis: Defined in CSS Text Decoration Module Level 4, `text-decoration-skip-spaces` provides granular author control over whether text decorations span whitespace characters, replacing brittle border hacks and pseudo-elements. Chromium led implementation with an enabled-by-default rollout in Chrome 155, but real-world web compatibility regressions regarding preserved single-space underlines prompted fresh CSS Working Group scrutiny. Consequently, cross-engine consensus on default values remains in flux, leaving broad multi-engine baseline support pending.

item.title: CSS position-visibility:anchor{s}-valid — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS position-visibility:anchor{s}-valid (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

The `anchors-valid` value was implemented as part of https://crbug.com/329703412 but subsequently reverted, due to spec questions about the exact definition of the value. Since that time, the value has been renamed to `anchor-valid` (see https://chromestatus.com/feature/5136123851571200) and also better defined to be clear that only the default anchor matters, resolving a lot of ambiguity, and making this value shippable.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS `position-visibility: anchor-valid` property (formerly `anchors-valid`) enables anchor-positioned elements such as menus and tooltips to be strongly hidden whenever their default anchor cannot be resolved, eliminating orphaned floating UI without manual JavaScript. Following CSS Working Group resolutions that clarified the specification to focus solely on the default anchor and standardized the singular syntax, the feature is set to ship enabled by default in Chromium 157. Engine consensus is aligned across the ecosystem, with Gecko and WebKit backing the clarified specification and supporting legacy plural aliases to safeguard web compatibility.

item.title: Pause media playback on not-visible iframes — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Pause media playback on not-visible iframes (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

Adds a "media-playback-while-not-visible" permission policy to allow embedders to pause audible media playback of embedded iframes which are currently hidden - i.e. "display" property set to "none"; "visibility" property set to "hidden"; or zero-area (width or height equal to 0). While hidden, attempts made by the embedded iframe to render audible media will be blocked. When the frame is shown again the prohibitions should be lifted. This should allow developers to build more user-friendly experiences and to also improve the performance by letting the browser handle the playback of content that is not visible to users.

Ecosystem Analysis: The 'Pause media playback on not-visible iframes' feature establishes the 'media-playback-while-not-visible' permissions policy, allowing web applications to pause audio and video inside embedded frames hidden via CSS display, visibility, or zero-dimension styling without tearing down the iframe element. Originating from Microsoft engineers within the WICG, the policy has shipped enabled by default in Chromium-based browsers, notably Chrome and Edge 155. Cross-engine alignment is advancing smoothly with positive feedback from Mozilla, while broader multi-engine standardization remains pending final WebKit consensus.

item.title: Long Animation Frames style and layout duration — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Long Animation Frames style and layout duration (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Add `styleDuration` and `forcedStyleDuration` information to the Long Animation Frame API, enabling developers to distinguish style and layout times.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API enhancement splits previously aggregated rendering metrics by introducing `styleDuration` and `layoutDuration` on frame entries, alongside `forcedStyleDuration` and `forcedLayoutDuration` on script entries. Enabled by default in Chromium-based browsers starting with Chrome and Microsoft Edge 157, the addition directly targets INP bottlenecks by disambiguating CSS selector overhead from DOM layout recalculations. However, cross-browser consensus remains lopsided, as the parent LoAF specification has yet to gain implementation traction in Gecko or WebKit.

item.title: WebTransport send groups and send-stream prioritization — Chrome 159 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport send groups and send-stream prioritization (Chrome 159, Enabled by default)

WebTransport already lets sites send data through WritableStreams. This feature lets applications assign outgoing streams to send groups and use sendOrder to prioritize streams within each group. It also provides sending statistics for streams and groups while preserving WritableStream transfer behavior.

Ecosystem Analysis: WebTransport send groups and send-stream prioritization address a critical multiplexing bottleneck by providing fair-share bandwidth allocation across groups alongside strict numeric sendOrder scheduling within groups. Standardized through the W3C WebTransport Working Group, this API is essential for advanced architectures such as Media over QUIC (MoQ) and high-frequency multiplayer gaming. With Chromium enabling the feature by default in Chrome 159 and Firefox adding support, the platform is moving toward deterministic transport scheduling.

item.title: WebTransport headers and responseHeaders — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport headers and responseHeaders (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

Adds support for passing custom HTTP request headers via WebTransportOptions and inspecting server response headers through the WebTransport instance. This allows web applications to supply metadata, authentication tokens, and custom parameters during the initial CONNECT handshake and access server-provided headers once the connection is established.

Ecosystem Analysis: Custom handshake headers and the companion responseHeaders property represent a major architectural maturity milestone for the WebTransport standard, formally specified by the W3C WebTransport Working Group to fix long-standing auth and routing gaps. With Chromium-based browsers shipping default support across Chrome and Microsoft Edge 156 and Mozilla landing implementation in Firefox 160, the feature resolves critical security concerns around token leakage in URLs and intermediaries. Developer perception is strongly favorable as it eliminates bespoke stream-level authentication handshakes and aligns WebTransport with standard reverse proxy architectures.

item.title: WebTransport Datagram readable stream type — Chrome 159 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport Datagram readable stream type (Chrome 159, Enabled by default)

Adds the  WebTransportOptions.datagramsReadableType  constructor option. By default, incoming WebTransport Datagrams are exposed through a default  ReadableStream . Applications that require BYOB reading can request a readable byte stream by setting  datagramsReadableType: "bytes" .

Ecosystem Analysis: The WebTransport Datagram readable stream type (`WebTransportOptions.datagramsReadableType`) standardizes control over whether incoming datagrams are exposed via a message-preserving default stream or an opt-in byte stream supporting zero-copy Bring Your Own Buffer (BYOB) readers. Scheduled to ship enabled by default in Chrome 159, the addition addresses longstanding developer friction around message boundary delineation and empty datagram loss. Engine consensus is exceptionally strong across the board, with active implementation and alignment across Chromium, Gecko, and WebKit.

item.title: Optional descriptors for registered custom properties — Chrome 159 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Optional descriptors for registered custom properties (Chrome 159, Enabled by default)

Allows authors to omit any descriptor in an @property rule and the corresponding optional members of CSS.registerProperty(). Omitted values default to universal syntax, inheritance, and the guaranteed-invalid initial value; invalid descriptors use normal CSS fallback behavior.

Ecosystem Analysis: The updated CSS Properties and Values API specification makes every descriptor in the `@property` rule and `CSS.registerProperty()` optional, defaulting omitted values to match standard custom property behavior—universal syntax (`*`), inheritance enabled (`true`), and a guaranteed-invalid initial value. Normatively resolved by the W3C CSS Working Group and led in implementation by Chromium, this change also establishes standard CSS fault-tolerant error recovery instead of discarding an entire rule on a single invalid descriptor. Beyond cutting repetitive boilerplate, it critically enables typed custom properties to work with per-use `var()` fallback values.

item.title: Margin-trim — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Margin-trim (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

The `margin-trim` CSS property may be used to omit margins before or after the first or last child of a container. This is supported on regular block containers and multicol containers. This is somewhat similar to the effect caused by the margin quirk that is applied to P, H1, H2... elements inside BODY and table cell elements (in quirks mode), but more powerful, generic, and expressive. Note: A previous version of the spec also applied this for flex and grid containers, but this has been removed.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `margin-trim` CSS property solves a longstanding layout challenge by allowing containers to trim extraneous child margins at container boundaries without requiring descendant pseudo-class overrides. Following early adoption in Safari 16.4, Chromium has enabled default support in Chrome 155, bringing the feature significantly closer to ubiquitous baseline availability. The CSS Working Group also recently streamlined the specification by focusing `margin-trim` specifically on block and multi-column containers while scoping it out of flex and grid containers.

item.title: CSS Symbols() — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS Symbols() (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

The CSS symbols() function lets authors define a counter style inline instead of first declaring a named @counter-style at-rule. It builds an anonymous counter style from a list of string symbols plus an optional counting system (cyclic, numeric, alphabetic, symbolic, or fixed), and is accepted as the counter style in list-style-type, the list-style shorthand, and counter() / counters().

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS symbols() function from CSS Counter Styles Level 3 enables authors to declare inline, anonymous counter styles directly inside properties like list-style-type without defining global @counter-style rules. With Blink enabling it by default in Chrome 155, the feature is finally closing a decade-old cross-engine interoperability gap alongside Mozilla Gecko's longstanding implementation. Consensus across browser engines is complete, with WebKit formally backing the specification and actively working on implementation patches.

item.title: AccentColor & AccentColorText follows accent-color value — Chrome 159 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
AccentColor & AccentColorText follows accent-color value (Chrome 159, Enabled by default)

`AccentColor` and `AccentColorText` reflect the element's effective `accent-color` value instead of only platform-provided system accent colors. This allows CSS to reference the same colors used by `accent-color` styling, making it easier to keep custom styling consistent with form controls and other accented UI. It aligns Chromium's behavior with the CSS Color Module Level 4 specification.

Ecosystem Analysis: The alignment of the `AccentColor` and `AccentColorText` system color keywords with the effective `accent-color` property fulfills a long-standing CSS Color Module Level 4 specification update, shipping enabled by default in Chrome 159. This resolves historical fingerprinting mitigations that either locked these keywords to static platform fallbacks or restricted them exclusively to installed web apps. With strong multi-engine backing across Chromium, Gecko, and WebKit, the feature establishes a standardized, dynamic link between form accent tokens and surrounding component styling.

item.title: Import Text (Text Modules) — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Import Text (Text Modules) (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

A TC39 proposal to add module `import … with { type: "text" }` statements to JavaScript. The import attribute loads text data as a string value.

Ecosystem Analysis: The TC39 Import Text proposal has rapidly matured at Stage 3, standardizing declarative text asset loading via `import ... with { type: 'text' }`. With Firefox shipping support in version 153 and Chromium enabling it by default in Chrome 155, the feature is close to full cross-browser interoperability. Developer sentiment is strongly favorable as native text modules eliminate historical reliance on bundler-specific plugins like raw-loader.

item.title: object-fit and object-position apply to SVG documents in <object> and <embed> — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
object-fit and object-position apply to SVG documents in <object> and <embed> (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

SVG documents loaded through <object> or <embed> are sized and positioned inside the element's content box according to the CSS object-fit and object-position properties, the same way <img> content is. Previously Chrome ignored both properties for embedded SVG documents and always stretched the document viewport to the whole content box.

Ecosystem Analysis: Chromium's support for applying object-fit and object-position to SVG documents loaded via <object> and <embed> tags resolves a decade-old inconsistency and aligns Chromium with the WHATWG and CSS Images specifications. While Firefox has supported this embedded-replaced element sizing behavior for years, Safari has historically stretched embedded SVGs across the container bounds. The move represents a major step forward for cross-engine interoperability, though WebKit implementation remains the final hurdle.

item.title: CSS text-overflow: <string> value — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS text-overflow: <string> value (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Adds a <string> value to the text-overflow property. This allows web authors to specify a custom string (e.g., "(more)") to indicate that text has been clipped. This provides more design flexibility and can be used to create more user-friendly and context-aware overflow indicators.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS `text-overflow: <string>` value allows web authors to define custom inline truncation markers (such as '(more)' or custom ellipsis symbols) without relying on fragile JavaScript truncation algorithms or pseudo-element overlays. Having been an isolated feature in Firefox since version 9 in 2011, its release enabled by default in Chrome 157 and its recent landing in WebKit trunk heralds broad multi-engine consensus. Developer reception is strongly favorable as it finally standardizes a long-sought styling capability across all major browser engines.

item.title: Use scroll-snap-type: pair to snap to a single element — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Use scroll-snap-type: pair to snap to a single element (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/9519 Add a "pair" keyword to scroll-snap-type. If used, when the container scroll snaps to an element on one axis, it should snap to the same element on the other axis. In the existing spec, the "both" keyword allows the scroll container to select snap targets in X and Y axes independently and snap to different targets.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `scroll-snap-type: pair` keyword resolves a longstanding limitation in CSS Scroll Snap Level 1 by requiring 2D scroll containers to snap to the same element along both axes rather than independently mismatching targets. Shipping enabled by default in Chrome 156 and proposed for Interop 2027, the addition enjoys strong cross-engine interest and standard track backing. The feature bridges a significant ergonomic gap for complex 2D viewports like maps, interactive galleries, and canvas-style layouts.

item.title: SpeechRecognitionResult Timestamps (WebSpeech API) — Chrome 159 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
SpeechRecognitionResult Timestamps (WebSpeech API) (Chrome 159, Enabled by default)

The Web Speech API currently does not expose the acoustic timing bounds of recognized speech segments, making it difficult to associate transcribed text with media timelines or generate synchronized subtitle cues. We propose adding speechStartTime and speechEndTime (double, in seconds relative to stream start) attributes on the SpeechRecognitionResult interface.

Ecosystem Analysis: The SpeechRecognitionResult Timestamps feature adds `speechStartTime` and `speechEndTime` properties to the Web Speech API, giving web applications precise acoustic bounds for transcribed speech segments. This resolves a major gap for automated WebVTT subtitling, interactive click-to-seek video navigation, and live conference synchronization. Chromium is shipping the feature enabled by default for desktop platforms using on-device speech recognition, while cross-engine standardization continues in the W3C Web Speech Community Group.

item.title: Digital Credentials API (issuance support) — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Digital Credentials API (issuance support) (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

This Web Platform feature enables issuing websites (e.g., a university, government agency, or bank) to securely initiate the provisioning (issuance) process of digital credentials directly into a user's mobile wallet application. On Android, this capability leverages the Android IdentityCredential CredMan system (Credential Manager). On Desktop, it leverages cross-device approaches using the CTAP protocol similar to Digital Credentials presentation.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Digital Credentials API issuance capability expands browser mediation beyond credential presentation to issuance via navigator.credentials.create(), shipping enabled by default in Chrome 155 on Android and desktop cross-device configurations. By leveraging native credential management systems like Android Credential Manager, the feature standardizes push provisioning for government IDs, mobile driver's licenses, and academic attestations. However, complete web ecosystem adoption remains gated by divergent engine consensus and ongoing concerns regarding digital identity tracking on the web.

item.title: WebTransport receive stream — Chrome 159 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport receive stream (Chrome 159, Enabled by default)

Adds the standardized WebTransportReceiveStream interface, a ReadableStream subclass used for incoming unidirectional streams and the readable side of bidirectional streams. Its getStats() method returns per-stream byte counters: bytesReceived reports bytes received from the network, while bytesRead reports bytes delivered to the application.

Ecosystem Analysis: The WebTransportReceiveStream interface standardizes incoming WebTransport unidirectional and bidirectional streams into a specialized ReadableStream subclass equipped with a stream-level getStats() method. This closes a key observability gap by exposing per-stream network counters (bytesReceived) alongside application-consumed counters (bytesRead) to identify reader bottlenecks and buffer bloat. With Chromium aligning with Safari and the W3C specification, and Firefox actively resolving test compliance, cross-engine interoperability for multiplexed transport diagnostics is rapidly stabilizing.

item.title: WebRTC Diagnostic Logging API — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebRTC Diagnostic Logging API (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

The Real-time Communication for the Web ([WebRTC](https://webrtc.org/)) Diagnostic Logging API allows authorized web applications to trigger the collection of WebRTC diagnostic data so that it can be used for local debugging. It also allows an application to share the WebRTC diagnostic data with the user agent vendor, subject to user authorization, with the purpose of providing information that can help fix bugs in or improve the user agent. Admins can enable diagnostic logs with the enterprise policy [WebRtcDiagnosticLogCollectionAllowedForOrigins](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcDiagnosticLogCollectionAllowedForOrigins).

Ecosystem Analysis: The WebRTC Diagnostic Logging API introduces web-exposed triggers to collect internal peer connection telemetry for local troubleshooting and browser vendor bug triage. Chromium is leading the rollout with general availability in Chrome 156, complemented by enterprise origin management policies. However, the ecosystem remains fractured because the feature lacks multi-engine consensus and is not yet on an interoperable standards track.

item.title: Single-axis scroll containers — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Single-axis scroll containers (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

Extends the `overflow` property to support scrollable values together with `clip` (for example, `overflow: scroll clip`). This allows `position: sticky` to be constrained by different ancestor scroll containers per axis, and gives authors a way to ensure an axis using `overflow: clip` stays in place.

Ecosystem Analysis: Single-axis scroll containers update CSS Overflow by permitting scrollable keywords (such as auto or scroll) to pair explicitly with clip, preventing the browser from coercing the clipped axis into a full two-dimensional scroller. This resolves the decade-old CSS issue where position: sticky elements inside horizontally scrolling containers were trapped by local overflow rather than sticking to the viewport or document scroll ancestors. While Chromium has shipped support enabled by default starting in Chrome 156 following TAG satisfaction, Mozilla Gecko and Apple WebKit standards positions remain active and open.

item.title: WebGPU: WGSL Fragment Depth — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebGPU: WGSL Fragment Depth (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

Adds the ability to provide a `less` or `greater` modifier to the `@builtin(frag_depth)` in WGSL. The current `@builtin(frag_depth)` can potentially introduce a performance penalty due to disabling the early-Z optimizations on a draw call. The new modifiers allow the explicit setting of the buffer mode and allow the early-Z optimizations to be applied.

Ecosystem Analysis: The WGSL `fragment_depth` extension introduces `less` and `greater` qualifiers to `@builtin(frag_depth)`, allowing GPUs to preserve early-Z depth rejection optimizations when fragment shaders write custom depth. Formally integrated into the W3C WebGPU Shading Language specification, the extension resolves a major performance penalty for depth-altering rendering effects like decals and parallax occlusion mapping. Chromium has shipped the capability in its 155–156 release cycle, though broad cross-engine availability remains pending.

item.title: WebTransport draining — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport draining (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

WebTransport.draining is a promise that resolves when the server indicates that the WebTransport session will be gracefully retired. Applications can use this signal to establish a replacement session while existing streams and the current session remain usable.

Ecosystem Analysis: WebTransport draining provides a promise-based notification mechanism that resolves when a server signals that an active WebTransport session is entering a graceful retirement phase. Standardized by W3C and IETF, the feature addresses critical connection lifecycle needs by enabling applications to establish replacement sessions in parallel without disrupting active streams. Shipping enabled by default in Chrome 158, engine consensus is strong, though non-Chromium engines are still completing protocol-level integration.

item.title: WebTransport reliability attributes — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport reliability attributes (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

Adds the WebTransport.reliability instance attribute and static WebTransport.supportsReliableOnly attribute. These APIs indicate whether the user agent supports WebTransport over exclusively reliable connections and whether an established session supports unreliable transport such as datagrams. In Chromium, reliability initially returns "pending" and changes to "supports-unreliable" after an HTTP/3 WebTransport connection is established.  Since Chromium does not currently support HTTP/2 fallback,  WebTransport.supportsReliableOnly returns false; any successfully established session uses HTTP/3 and supports unreliable datagrams.

Ecosystem Analysis: The WebTransport reliability attributes introduce the static supportsReliableOnly property and session-level reliability attribute, allowing web applications to detect whether an engine or active session supports unreliable datagrams or exclusively reliable streams. Formalized in the W3C WebTransport Candidate Recommendation, these APIs address critical feature-detection requirements as HTTP/2 fallback mechanisms enter the networking landscape. Engine consensus is strong across vendors, establishing an essential diagnostic foundation for real-time media and low-latency interactive applications.

item.title: Web haptics JavaScript API — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Web haptics JavaScript API (Chrome 156, In developer trial (Behind a flag))

Provides a JavaScript API for triggering semantic haptic feedback, such as hints, ticks, alignment confirmations, and boundary signals. User agents translate these semantic effects into platform-appropriate haptic feedback based on the available hardware and operating system.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Web Haptics API is an emerging WICG incubation led by Microsoft Edge engineers designed to replace low-level vibration patterns with semantic, intent-driven tactile feedback like ticks, hints, and boundary signals. Currently available as an experimental developer trial in Chromium 156 (behind a feature flag on Windows 11), it encompasses both an imperative JavaScript method (`navigator.playHaptics()`) and an experimental declarative CSS proposal. However, consensus remains nascent, with Safari and Firefox registering no official signals and standards bodies actively debating declarative triggering models.
